question: Place \(m\) \(1 \times 2\) dominos on a \(7\times7\) chessboard such that no domino can slide horizontally or vertically when other dominos remains fixed. Find the minimal possible value of \(m\).
skills: domino sliding constraint analysis, ILP formulation, lower bound via blocking argument
why_wrong: The dominant wrong answer is 8 (12/32 attempts in v31 runs). Attempts that get 8 misinterpret the sliding constraint: they assume a domino can only slide along its own orientation (horizontal domino slides left/right only, vertical slides up/down only). Under this restricted interpretation, far fewer dominos are needed. The correct interpretation is that ANY domino can slide in ANY of the 4 directions (left, right, up, down) as a rigid translation, preserving orientation. A horizontal domino at (r,c)-(r,c+1) can slide up to (r-1,c)-(r-1,c+1) if both target cells are empty, or down similarly. This perpendicular sliding constraint dramatically increases the number of dominos needed. Attempts also commonly try ILP with pulp/ortools (unavailable), fall back to heuristic search, and find local optima that are not global minima.
correct_approach: The correct approach has two parts: (1) Use scipy.optimize.milp or exhaustive backtracking search to find a valid configuration with 22 dominos, and (2) prove that 21 is infeasible (also via ILP or exhaustive search). The key constraint formulation: for each domino, ALL 4 sliding directions must be blocked. For a horizontal domino at (r,c)-(r,c+1), blocking left requires (r,c-1) occupied or off-board, blocking right requires (r,c+2) occupied or off-board, blocking up requires BOTH (r-1,c) and (r-1,c+1) occupied or off-board, blocking down requires BOTH (r+1,c) and (r+1,c+1) occupied or off-board. This is an ILP with binary variables for each possible domino placement and constraints ensuring mutual blocking. The answer is 22 dominos covering 44 of 49 squares.
what_correct_attempts_did: All 7 correct attempts used ILP-style formulation (scipy.optimize.milp since pulp/ortools unavailable) with explicit blocking constraints in all 4 directions. They had significantly more code (15K chars avg vs 10K wrong) and more turns (45 vs 26), indicating iterative refinement. They verified both feasibility at 22 and infeasibility at 21. The critical differentiator was correctly modeling perpendicular sliding (a horizontal domino can slide up/down if BOTH cells above/below are empty).

question: How many squares at least should be marked on a \(13\times13\) chessboard such that for any placement of a bishop on the chessboard, the bishop can threaten at least one of the marked squares? (A bishop can threaten the squares on the same diagonal line, and if a bishop is placed on a marked square, it is also considered that the square is threatened.)
skills: diagonal covering, bipartite graph edge domination, distinguishing diagonal families
why_wrong: NEVER CORRECT across 48 attempts (0/48). The dominant wrong answer is 13 (18/32 attempts). The model consistently reduces the problem to: 'cover all 25 NW-SE diagonals and all 25 NE-SW diagonals, such that for each square, at least one of its two diagonals contains a marked square.' It then correctly observes that covering 13 diagonals from one family suffices (since the 13x13 board has 25 diagonals per family, and the 13 longest ones cover all squares). With one marked square per diagonal, this gives 13. However, this analysis has a critical flaw: it treats the problem as a vertex cover on the bipartite diagonal graph, when it is actually an EDGE DOMINATING SET problem. The difference is that a marked square on diagonal d covers all squares on diagonal d AND all squares sharing the OTHER diagonal with any square on d. The model fails to account for the interaction between the two diagonal families: a bishop on square (i,j) threatens all squares on BOTH diagonals through (i,j), not just one. The correct formulation requires that each square shares at least one diagonal with a marked square, which is more restrictive than just covering 13 diagonals. Specifically, corner diagonals of length 1 need special treatment: the single square on a length-1 diagonal must itself be marked OR share its other diagonal with a marked square.
correct_approach: This is an edge dominating set problem on the bipartite graph where vertices are diagonals (25 NW-SE + 25 NE-SW) and edges are board squares (each square connects its two diagonals). A set of marked squares M is valid iff every edge (square) either is in M or shares a vertex (diagonal) with an edge in M. The minimum edge dominating set of this bipartite graph has size 24 for n=13. To solve computationally: formulate as ILP with a binary variable per square, constraint that for each square (i,j), at least one square sharing a diagonal with (i,j) is marked. Use scipy.optimize.milp. The key insight that 13 is wrong: consider the 4 corner squares. Each corner lies on two length-1 diagonals. If neither length-1 diagonal has a marked square on it, then the corner is only covered if its length-13 diagonal has a marked square. But the corner's length-1 diagonal ALSO needs coverage for other squares. The interaction between short and long diagonals forces the count up to 24.
what_correct_attempts_did: No attempts got this correct across either version. The model needs to either (a) formulate the correct ILP and solve it with scipy.optimize.milp, or (b) recognize this as an edge dominating set problem and compute it for small n to find the pattern, then extrapolate to n=13. The brute-force approach for small boards (n=1..6 giving sequence 1,2,3,4,5,6) is misleading because the pattern breaks for larger n.

question: An explorer is challenging to pass through a maze composed of 3033 rows and 3032 columns of squares. The rules of the maze are as follows: In all the middle rows (that is, from the 2nd row to the 3032nd row), there is one invisible teleportation gate hidden in each row, and there are no multiple invisible teleportation gates in the same column. The explorer starts from any position in the 1st row. Each time, he can move one square up, down, left or right, and it is allowed to pass through the explored areas repeatedly. If the explorer touches a teleportation gate, he will immediately return to the starting point and start the next attempt. However, the explorer will mark the position of that teleportation gate. If the explorer reaches any position in the 3033rd row, he will directly pass the maze. It is known that the explorer can remember the positions of all the discovered teleportation gates. Please construct a general strategy so that no matter how the teleportation gates are distributed, the explorer will definitely pass the maze in the \(k\)th attempt in the worst-case scenario. Find the minimum possible value of \(k\).
skills: adaptive exploration strategy, information-theoretic lower bound, column-avoidance zigzag
why_wrong: The dominant wrong answer is 3032 (21/32 attempts). Nearly all attempts reason as follows: there are 3031 gates in 3032 columns, one column is gate-free (safe). Each attempt reveals at most one gate's column. Therefore you need to discover 3031 gate columns to identify the safe one, requiring 3031+1=3032 attempts. This reasoning has a fundamental flaw: it assumes each attempt can only discover ONE gate (the one you step on). In reality, the explorer can NAVIGATE AROUND known gates in subsequent attempts, using horizontal movement in gate-free rows to switch columns and traverse multiple rows per attempt. After discovering gate positions in previous attempts, the explorer can plan a path that avoids known gates and reaches much deeper into the maze. The key insight is that discovering even 1-2 gates gives enough information to navigate the entire maze by switching columns at the right rows.
correct_approach: The answer is 3 (logarithmic, not linear). Strategy: (1) Attempt 1: walk straight down column c1. Either succeed (c1 is safe) or discover gate at (r1, c1). (2) Attempt 2: walk down column c2 (different from c1). If c2 is safe, succeed. Otherwise discover gate at (r2, c2). Now you know two gate positions. (3) Attempt 3: start in column c1 or c2, walk down to just above the known gate row, move horizontally to the other column (avoiding the gate), continue down. If you hit a gate at (r3, c3) where c3 is c1 or c2, that is impossible because you already know those gates. The key insight: after 2 failures, you know gate positions in 2 columns. You can navigate through ANY row by choosing whichever of those 2 columns does NOT have a gate at that row. Since each row has exactly one gate, and the two known gates are in different rows, you can always find a safe path down by zigzagging between the two columns, switching at the rows where you know gates exist. This guarantees success on attempt 3. Lower bound proof: 2 attempts are not sufficient because after 1 failure you know only 1 gate, and the adversary can place gates to block any single-column strategy on the 2nd attempt.
what_correct_attempts_did: The one correct attempt (v31, attempt 3, temp=0.3) used extended pure reasoning (54,788 chars vs 17,648 avg for wrong). It explored the problem much more deeply, considering the explorer's ability to use horizontal movement and switch between columns. It proved that after discovering 2 gates, the explorer can always find a path by zigzagging between the two known columns. The critical difference: wrong attempts assume 'each attempt reveals at most one gate' as the bottleneck, while the correct attempt realized 'after 2 known gates, you can navigate the ENTIRE maze by column-switching.'

question: Kevin throws three fair dice numbered from 1 to 6. Then he observes the results of the first throw of the three dice. From these three dice, he can choose \(n\), where \(0\leq n\leq3\) dice to re-throw once. After that, the operation ends. Kevin's goal is to maximize the probability that the sum of the numbers on the final three dice is 7, and Kevin is smart enough. Let the probability when \(n = 2\) be \(p\). What is the value of \(216\times p\)?
skills: conditional probability, optimal strategy enumeration, careful problem reading
why_wrong: The dominant wrong answer is 95 (19/32 attempts). The model misinterprets 'the probability when n=2' as 'the probability of achieving sum 7 when Kevin re-throws exactly 2 dice (given he always re-throws 2).' Under this interpretation, p = 95/864 and 216p = 95/4 = 23.75, which the model rounds or reports as 95. The CORRECT interpretation is: 'p is the probability that Kevin's OPTIMAL strategy involves re-throwing exactly 2 dice.' Kevin is smart and chooses n optimally for each initial roll. The question asks: across all 216 equally likely initial rolls, in how many cases does the optimal choice happen to be n=2? That count divided by 216 is p, so 216p is the count itself. The model computes the probability OF GETTING SUM 7 when n=2, rather than the probability OF CHOOSING n=2 when playing optimally.
correct_approach: For each of the 216 possible initial rolls (a,b,c), compute the probability of achieving sum=7 for each choice of n=0,1,2,3, then determine which n is optimal. Count the number of initial rolls where n=2 is optimal. Computation: (1) n=0: sum=7 iff a+b+c=7. Probability = 1 if sum=7, else 0. (2) n=1: keep 2 dice, re-throw 1. For each kept pair, probability sum=7 is (# of values for re-thrown die making total=7)/6. Choose which die to re-throw to maximize this. (3) n=2: keep 1 die with value v, re-throw 2. Probability both new dice sum to 7-v is (6-|7-v-3.5|... actually count pairs summing to 7-v from 2d6). Keep the die giving highest probability, which is the smallest die (value closest to 1, giving target 6 for two dice = 5 ways out of 36). (4) n=3: re-throw all, probability = 15/216. For each triple, find max probability across n=0,1,2,3. Count triples where n=2 wins. Result: n=0 optimal for 15 triples, n=1 for 132, n=2 for 42, n=3 for 27. So 216p = 42.
what_correct_attempts_did: Correct attempts (5 in v23, 2 in v31) explicitly enumerated all 216 triples, computed optimal n for each, and counted those where n=2 is optimal. They recognized the ambiguity in 'probability when n=2' and tested both interpretations: (a) probability of sum=7 given n=2, vs (b) probability that optimal n is 2. Finding that interpretation (a) gives non-integer 95/4, and the problem requires an integer answer, they correctly chose interpretation (b) = 42. The key differentiator: wrong attempts never check whether their answer is a valid integer, despite the problem explicitly requiring 'a non-negative integer between 0 and 99999.'

question: The Bank of Pittsburgh issues coins that have a heads side and a tails side. Vera has a row of 7873 such coins alternately tails-up and heads-up, with the leftmost coin tails-up. In a move, Vera may flip over one of the coins in the row, subject to the following rules: • On the first move, Vera may flip over any of the 7873 coins. • On all subsequent moves, Vera may only flip over a coin adjacent to the coin she flipped on the previous move. (We do not consider a coin to be adjacent to itself.) Determine the smallest possible number of moves Vera can make to reach a state in which every coin is heads-up.
skills: parity constraint analysis, modular arithmetic on edge traversals, small-case verification
why_wrong: The dominant wrong answer is 15743 (10/32 attempts), off by exactly 1 from the correct answer 15744. Attempts correctly identify that the problem reduces to finding minimum total edge traversals on a path graph of 7873 vertices, subject to parity constraints (each coin must be flipped an odd number of times for T->H, even for H->T). They derive a formula like 2N-3 where N=7873, giving 15743. The off-by-one error comes from miscounting boundary conditions: either (a) miscounting whether the formula should be 2N-3 or 2N-2, (b) incorrectly handling the first/last coin's parity constraint, or (c) using the wrong initial state pattern (THTH... vs THTTH...). The correct formula gives 2*7872 = 15744. The model does NOT verify its formula on small cases (N=3,5,7) before extrapolating, which would catch the off-by-one.
correct_approach: Model as a walk on positions 1..7873. Each move flips one coin and moves to an adjacent position. The walk is a sequence of positions where consecutive positions differ by 1. Each position i is visited some number of times v_i; coin i flips v_i times. Need: v_i odd if coin i starts T (odd positions: 1,3,5,...), v_i even if coin i starts H (even positions: 2,4,6,...). Total moves = sum of edge traversals. Key insight: consider edge (i, i+1). Each traversal of this edge contributes 1 to both v_i and v_{i+1}. Let x_i = number of times edge (i,i+1) is traversed. Then v_i = x_{i-1} + x_i (with x_0 = x_N = 0 for boundary). Parity constraints: x_{i-1} + x_i must be odd for odd i, even for even i. This gives x_i mod 2 follows a periodic pattern. Minimum total = sum of minimum positive x_i satisfying the modular constraints. For N=7873 (which is 1 mod 4), the pattern of minimum edge counts is periodic with period 4: {1, 3, 3, 1, 1, 3, 3, 1, ...}. Each period of 4 edges sums to 8. There are 7872 edges = 1968 full periods. Total = 1968 * 8 = 15744. CRITICAL: verify on small cases first. For N=3: minimum is 4 moves (not 3). For N=5: minimum is 8 moves. Pattern: 4*(N-1)/2 = 2*(N-1). For N=7873: 2*7872 = 15744.
what_correct_attempts_did: The one correct attempt (v31, attempt 5, temp=0.3) used extensive pure reasoning (99,879 chars, far more than the 68,972 avg for wrong). It carefully worked out the edge traversal formulation, computed the modular constraints, identified the period-4 pattern {1,3,3,1}, and computed the total as 4*3936 = 15744. The key differentiator from wrong attempts: it explicitly verified the pattern on small cases and correctly handled the boundary conditions at positions 1 and N, rather than jumping to a formula like 2N-3 without verification.

question: Let \(G\) be a 160-order simple graph. For any vertex \(u\), there exists another vertex \(v\), such that \(u\) and \(v\) are adjacent, and there exists no vertices adjacent to both \(u\) and \(v\). Find the maximal number of edges in \(G\).
skills: triangle-free edge condition, core-leaf decomposition, complete multipartite optimization
why_wrong: The dominant wrong answer is 6400 (14/32 attempts). Attempts interpret the condition as 'each vertex has a neighbor with no common neighbor', which means each vertex is incident to at least one triangle-free edge (an edge not contained in any triangle). They then incorrectly conclude the graph must be triangle-free itself, applying Turan's theorem for triangle-free graphs: max edges = floor(n^2/4) = floor(160^2/4) = 6400. This is wrong because the condition only requires EACH VERTEX to have AT LEAST ONE triangle-free edge, not that ALL edges be triangle-free. The graph can contain many triangles, as long as every vertex also has at least one triangle-free neighbor. This allows far more edges than a triangle-free graph. The model typically uses pure reasoning (avg 4.1 turns) and arrives at 6400 without considering constructions that include triangles.
correct_approach: Use a core-leaf decomposition. Partition vertices into 'core' vertices (forming a clique or dense subgraph) and 'leaf' vertices (each attached to exactly one core vertex via a triangle-free edge). Core vertices: k vertices forming a complete graph K_k. Each core vertex has at least one 'private' leaf (a leaf neighbor not adjacent to any other core vertex neighbor). The leaf's only core neighbor has a triangle-free edge to the leaf. Leaves of DIFFERENT core vertices can be connected (since those edges may be in triangles, but the leaf still has its triangle-free edge to its core vertex). Optimal structure: k core vertices, each with ~(n-k)/k leaves, all cross-group leaf edges present (complete multipartite on leaves). Total edges = C(k,2) + k*s + sum of cross-group edges. Optimize over k. For n=160: optimal k=9 core vertices with leaf groups of sizes [17,17,17,17,17,17,17,16,16] (151 leaves total). Edges = C(9,2) + 151 + [C(151,2) - sum C(s_i,2)] = 36 + 151 + 11325 - 7*C(17,2) - 2*C(16,2) = 36 + 151 + 11325 - 952 - 240 = 10320.
what_correct_attempts_did: Both correct attempts (v31, attempts 3 and 14) recognized that the graph can contain triangles and developed the core-leaf partition idea. They set up the optimization: maximize total edges as a function of core size k and leaf distribution, subject to each core vertex having at least one private leaf. Attempt 3 (temp=0.3, 25 turns) used extensive computation to verify the formula. Attempt 14 (temp=0.7, 11 turns) also derived the same structure. Both found k=9 as optimal, with leaf sizes balanced as evenly as possible (7 groups of 17, 2 of 16). The key insight: the complete multipartite structure on leaves maximizes edges while preserving triangle-free edges between each leaf and its core vertex.
